title: Bulk structural solids at a large fraction of ideal strength

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a bulk structural material that carries tensile stress approaching a large fraction of its own ideal crystal strength while retaining useful resistance to cracks. Ideal tensile strength describes the limit calculated for a specified defect-free crystal under specified loading conditions. Reaching a substantial fraction of that limit in a useful component requires controlling the mechanisms that ordinarily cause yielding or fracture much earlier.

The central challenge is the combination of strength, flaw tolerance, and bulk size. Dislocation nucleation and motion, microcracks, and microstructural features govern practical failure. Interfaces can strengthen a material by obstructing deformation, but their effects depend on their structure and behavior; their presence does not automatically weaken a solid. Results from very small, nearly defect-free stressed volumes do not by themselves establish equivalent performance in a structural section.

Four quantities must remain distinct. Ideal tensile strength is a calculated crystal limit; yield strength marks the onset of substantial permanent deformation; tensile ductility measures deformation before tensile failure; and fracture toughness characterizes resistance to crack extension under specified conditions. High yield strength or appreciable tensile elongation alone does not establish that a material can tolerate a pre-existing crack at a high applied stress.

significance.text: Achieving high usable stress together with measured flaw tolerance would address a central structural-materials limitation: a material must withstand service loads while resisting failure from imperfections. The revolutionary feature would be bringing a substantial portion of ideal-crystal strength into a bulk section whose fracture behavior is also demonstrated. The 2025 perspective identifies fracture toughness, fatigue endurance, and processability under complex loading as remaining challenges despite gains in strength and ductility.

Engineering synthesis: higher allowable tensile stresses could permit smaller load-bearing sections or higher internal pressures for a given component geometry. Lighter load paths would additionally require favorable density and acceptable stiffness, buckling resistance, fatigue performance, and safety margins. These are conditional design consequences, not application results demonstrated by the supplied sources.

Engineering synthesis: broader possibilities include lighter machinery and more demanding structural or pressure-containing systems, provided the material can be manufactured, joined, inspected, and maintained at useful cost. A high fraction of ideal strength alone would not establish the feasibility of a space elevator or another extreme structure. Such systems impose additional requirements on specific strength, scale, durability, joints, and service environment that the proposed material benchmark does not resolve.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is a reproducible way to suppress premature deformation and fracture throughout a bulk section while preserving mechanisms that prevent unstable crack growth. Strengthening by restricting dislocation motion can improve load capacity, but preserving tensile deformation and fracture resistance remains a separate challenge. The supplied evidence supports this combined problem without identifying a processing route that solves it.

Size matters because idealized calculations and small defect-free stressed volumes do not represent the full defect population and microstructural variability of bulk material. A convincing advance must maintain its favorable structure across a useful section and show how cracks behave under load. The supplied sources ground this size concern qualitatively; they do not establish a quantitative scaling law connecting specimen size to attainable strength.

A further barrier is defining a physically meaningful ideal-strength reference. The calculation must specify composition, crystal structure, loading direction, stress definition, temperature, and boundary conditions, including whether transverse dimensions relax. A tensile stress maximum also needs interpretation in light of competing instabilities that could occur earlier. Otherwise, an apparent percentage of ideal strength could reflect mismatched reference conditions rather than a meaningful materials advance.

Engineering synthesis: practical deployment would additionally require control of processing defects, reproducible production, and retention of useful properties after component fabrication and joining. Fatigue endurance, multiaxial loading, and service conditions require their own evidence; success in a room-temperature monotonic tensile test would establish only part of the necessary capability.

current_state.text: In 2003, M. Friák, M. Šob, and V. Vitek reported first-principles ideal tensile strengths of 12.7 GPa for loading along [001] and 27.3 GPa along [111] in ferromagnetic body-centered-cubic iron. These are calculated ideal-crystal results, not measured strengths of bulk structural specimens. Their strong orientation dependence illustrates why the reference for an ideal-strength fraction must be explicitly defined. The paper also discusses calculation boundary conditions and the possibility of an earlier competing instability.

En Ma’s 2025 Science Advances perspective describes alloy-design and heterogeneous-nanostructure progress that improves strength–ductility combinations, including alloys strengthened to approximately 2 GPa. It presents yield strengths well above 2.3 GPa without much loss of ductility as a next challenge, rather than as a result established by that statement. This article summarizes other work; it is not itself a primary mechanical-test report. Its discussion of tensile ductility does not establish corresponding fracture toughness.

The calculations and perspective establish a useful scale comparison between ideal iron tensile strengths and bulk-alloy yield strengths around a few gigapascals. They do not provide a direct, like-for-like performance ratio: ideal tensile strength and alloy yield strength are different quantities, and the materials and loading conditions differ. Neither supplied text establishes a section satisfying the proposed combination of bulk dimensions, ideal-strength fraction, and resistance to a specified pre-crack.

The earlier research account reported unavailable repeat full-text fetches. The supplied review subsequently assessed an identity-verified, complete retained PDF of the iron paper and complete article XML for the 2025 perspective. The review found the relevant prose and tables sufficient for the claims above despite PDF text-extraction artifacts; the perspective’s figure graphics were not inspected. These statements summarize that supplied review and do not imply a new inspection of either document.

Evidence limitation: no freshness-search entries were supplied to establish the worldwide state of the field through 2026-11-01. The 2003 calculation and 2025 perspective remain informative at their stated dates, but the absence of a qualifying demonstration in these two sources does not prove that no such material exists. The combined innovation remains unestablished by the supplied evidence.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed benchmark: at room temperature, demonstrate an Earth-abundant material with a minimum section dimension of 5 mm sustaining at least 50% of a carefully defined, computed ideal uniaxial tensile strength. Earth abundance, 5 mm, and 50% are proposed choices for this record, not thresholds prescribed by the sources or established community standards.
completion_criteria.label: Room-temperature 5 mm Earth-abundant sections sustain ≥50% ideal tensile strength

completion_criteria.text: The ideal reference should specify the relevant composition, crystal structure, orientation, stress definition, temperature, and boundary conditions. The comparison should explain any mismatch between the calculation and experiment, including transverse relaxation and possible competing instabilities. The iron calculations support the need for these qualifications, rather than endorsing a particular percentage threshold.
completion_criteria.label: Fully specify ideal-strength references and explain calculation–experiment mismatches

completion_criteria.text: Proposed flaw-tolerance demonstration: separately test a specified 0.5 mm pre-crack in the same material condition used for the strength demonstration. Before testing, define crack geometry and orientation, loading mode, applied load, and an acceptable crack-growth or failure threshold. Resistance under an unspecified load would not provide an assessable pass condition. Separate specimens may be needed, but unrelated material conditions should not satisfy the combined strength and toughness goal.
completion_criteria.label: Same-condition material passes predefined 0.5 mm pre-crack resistance tests

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reporting and reproducibility requirements: report specimen dimensions, processing and material condition, orientation, loading rate, temperature, stress–strain behavior, measured fracture toughness and its validity limits, sample counts, and statistical variability. Repeat the combined demonstration across independently produced batches and seek independent replication. These measures would help distinguish a reproducible bulk capability from an exceptional specimen.
completion_criteria.label: Report measurements and variability; reproduce combined demonstration across independent batches

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: state the demonstrated ranges of section size, orientation, loading mode, rate, and temperature, and identify untested service conditions. Application-specific qualification should examine fatigue, multiaxial loads, fabrication, and joining where relevant. Finite testing would establish demonstrated breadth within those boundaries; it would not establish universal flaw tolerance or suitability for every structure.
completion_criteria.label: State demonstrated operating boundaries and identify untested service conditions

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: MEC-04, Ambient fatigue immunity in bulk structural metals, is closely related because fatigue endurance is another limit on high-stress structural service. MEC-07 concerns high tensile strength together with measured crack resistance; it does not establish immunity to damage under repeated loading. MEC-11, Transferable prediction of wear and component life, and MEC-12, Predictive mechanics of real, evolving surface contacts, concern prediction of degradation and contact behavior. They could help qualify applications of a new material, while remaining distinct from creating that material.

Roster-based synthesis: MEC-06, Macroscopic atomically precise mechanosynthesis, could conceivably provide routes to controlled structures or defects, but atomically precise fabrication would not itself demonstrate bulk strength and toughness. MEC-05, Programmable solids that become different load-bearing mechanisms, and MEC-10, Stress-directed growth of load-bearing structures, concern changing structural behavior or geometry. They might incorporate strong materials, but their defining capabilities differ from the material performance sought here.

Roster-based synthesis: MEC-13, General-purpose synthesis of practical mechanisms, concerns mechanism design, while MEC-09, Mechanical self-replication of a production cell from feedstock, concerns production capability. Either could use or manufacture improved structural materials, but neither inherently satisfies MEC-07. MEC-08, Distributed actuators that simultaneously match skeletal muscle, could benefit from strong load-bearing elements, although actuator performance also depends on capabilities beyond passive material strength.

Roster-based synthesis: MEC-02, Service-life superlubricity in ordinary machine contacts, addresses friction and contact durability. MEC-03, Engines that make sub-100 °C heat worth converting, and MEC-14, Low-cost mechanical storage with high efficiency over long periods, address energy conversion or storage performance. Stronger structural solids could be enabling components in these systems, but would not establish their respective breakthroughs. MEC-01, An engineering-predictive theory of turbulent flow, concerns predictive fluid mechanics and has only an indirect connection through the design of structures exposed to fluid loads.

unresolved_issues: Whether any material outside the supplied evidence meets the combined benchmark remains unresolved; no freshness-search entries establish worldwide nonachievement through 2026-11-01.
The proposed crack test still needs a selected geometry, loading mode, applied load, and numerical acceptance threshold before it can be executed as a pass/fail demonstration.

No target material or ideal-strength calculation protocol has been selected; composition, orientation, temperature, stress definition, boundary conditions, and competing instabilities must be resolved for a specific comparison.
The rationale for the proposed 50% strength fraction, 5 mm section dimension, 0.5 mm pre-crack, and operational definition of Earth abundance remains to be developed for an intended application.

Primary experimental reports underlying the 2025 perspective were not supplied for detailed assessment of specimen dimensions, statistical variability, or fracture toughness; its figure graphics were not inspected in the supplied review.

brief.title: Strong bulk materials that resist cracks
possible: Machinery could carry the same loads with smaller supporting parts. Pressure-containing components could withstand higher internal pressures. The goal is a material that approaches the strength of a perfect crystal while still resisting the spread of cracks through a useful-sized part.
why: Real materials often deform or break well before their atoms reach their load-bearing limit. Combining much higher usable strength with resistance to cracks would let engineers carry heavier loads without making parts proportionally larger.

sources.who: M. Friák, M. Šob and V. Vitek
sources.showed: They calculated the pulling strength of defect-free iron and found that it depends strongly on the direction of pulling within the crystal.
sources.quote:
The total energy dependences have a parabolic convex character in the neigh-
bourhood of the symmetry-dictated minimum in the bcc structure (ground state).
sources.cited_for: A material’s ideal strength—the calculated limit for a perfect crystal—needs a precisely defined loading direction and test conditions.
sources.not_established: Calculating perfect-crystal strength does not demonstrate a bulk material that approaches it while resisting cracks.

sources.showed: This perspective reviews alloys, or mixtures of metals, that combine high strength with substantial stretching before failure. It summarizes other researchers’ experiments.
sources.quote: Lending support to this perspective is the observation that the compressive ductility of alloys is mostly uncompromised even when strengthened to 2 GPa.
sources.cited_for: Alloys can become much stronger while retaining the ability to deform, which helps with shaping and forming.
sources.not_established: Stretching before failure does not establish resistance to an existing crack, or strength close to the material’s perfect-crystal limit.

shown: En Ma’s review describes bulk alloys reaching about 2 gigapascals in yield strength—the stress where substantial permanent deformation begins—while retaining considerable stretching before failure. That advances the combination of strength and formability; resistance to existing cracks remains a separate question.

Friák and colleagues calculated perfect iron’s strength and its dependence on pulling direction. Those calculations and the alloy results cannot be turned into a direct percentage: they concern different materials and different measures of strength.
missing: A bulk material must combine a large fraction of its perfect-crystal strength with measured resistance to an existing crack.
A production method must preserve that combination throughout a useful section and across independently made batches.
The strength calculation and physical test must use meaningfully comparable material and loading conditions.

milestones.label: Bulk sections sustain half their ideal strength
milestones.explanation: A material made from abundant elements would have to sustain 50% of its calculated perfect-crystal strength at room temperature and the specified bulk thickness. This would bring the strength into a useful-sized section.

milestones.label: Calculated and measured strength have a meaningful comparison
milestones.explanation: The calculation would have to define the material, crystal direction and loading conditions, and explain differences from the experiment or earlier failure mechanisms. This would make the claimed strength fraction meaningful.

milestones.label: The same material condition resists a specified crack
milestones.explanation: The same material condition would have to pass a test with a 0.5 mm pre-existing crack, with geometry, loading and acceptable crack growth defined beforehand. This would establish assessable resistance to flaws.

milestones.label: Independent batches reproduce the combined performance
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to report strength, resistance to crack growth, specimen and test details, and variability across independent batches, with independent replication sought. This would distinguish reproducible performance from an exceptional sample.

milestones.label: Tests establish the limits of demonstrated performance
milestones.explanation: Results would have to state tested sizes, directions, loads, rates and temperatures, and identify untested service conditions. This would define where the performance applies and what further application testing remains.

uncertain: The proposed strength, size and crack thresholds still need a rationale tied to an intended use, alongside a definition of abundant elements.
The crack test still needs a chosen geometry, applied load and numerical pass condition.
It remains unclear which material and production route could deliver the combined strength and crack resistance at bulk size.

page.title: Bulk metals with deep ultra-strength and stable crack growth
page.definition: A crystalline metal in a standard 12.5 mm diameter tensile specimen sustains more than half its ideal tensile strength and, in the same material condition, exhibits stable crack growth. Ideal strength is the instability stress of the corresponding defect-free crystal; stable crack growth arrests when applied displacement is held fixed.

goal.need: Calculated ideal tensile strengths of ferromagnetic iron are 12.7 GPa along [001] and 27.3 GPa along [111]. A 2025 perspective places the bulk-alloy yield-strength envelope near 2.3 GPa; these different materials and strength measures cannot establish an ideal-strength fraction. Pearlitic steel-wire fracture toughness varies by factors of 5–8 with crack direction. A strength increase therefore requires a separate demonstration of crack resistance.

figures.caption: Crack-direction dependence in pearlitic steel wires, published on 14 September 2016.
figures.note: Two specimens per material condition and crack-growth direction. For the approximately 24 μm wires, perpendicular-direction values are lower bounds rather than pure mode-I toughness because cracks deflected. The specimens contained focused-ion-beam notches.

statements.body: European Research Council-funded Ultra Strong Materials programme, Austrian Academy of Sciences
statements.quote: The improvement of strength and toughness is one of the main goals in materials science.
statements.context: The final report concerns pearlitic steel wires and transferring their strength–ductility combinations to other metal-based nanocomposites.

statements.body: JSPS International Leading Research programme on structural metallic materials, Kyoto University
statements.quote: The present project aims to realize metals and alloys with both ultra-high strength and high toughness/ductility through their nano-structuring.
statements.context: Project 23K20037 pursues bulk nanostructured metals using controlled deformation mechanisms.

completion.title: A bulk metal exceeds half its ideal tensile strength and exhibits stable growth from fatigue precracks.
completion.criterion: At a common temperature within 10–38 °C, a metal in the published ASTM round geometry—initial diameter 12.5 ± 0.2 mm and gauge length 62.5 ± 0.1 mm—reaches true axial stress above 0.5 times its ideal tensile strength. The reference is a 0 K defect-free crystal with matched composition, phase and loading direction, with transverse relaxation and competing instabilities assessed. Separate specimens in the same material condition and orientation exhibit stable tearing from fatigue precracks under ASTM E1820: crack extension beyond blunting arrests when displacement is held constant, and a qualified crack-resistance curve is obtained.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback combining the published deep ultra-strength definition, ASTM E8M-01e1 round-specimen geometry and ASTM E1820-21 stable-tearing definition; no cited body adopted this conjunction.
completion.basis: Searches of ERC USMS objectives and final reporting, JSPS project 23K20037, and ASTM tensile and fracture documents found no combined achievement test. This fallback joins an externally published strength fraction, specimen geometry and physical fracture response. The specimen geometry supplies an explicit size; stable tearing supplies an observable crack-resistance outcome. Neither supplies an application-specific minimum toughness.

milestones.title: A crystalline metal sustains more than one-tenth of its matched ideal strength.
milestones.criterion: A specimen sustains specimen-wide stress above 0.1 times the ideal strength for the corresponding loading mode. Tensile and shear comparisons remain separate. Wang and colleagues reported more than 20 gold-nanowire tests, with diameters of 8–20 nm, on 23 April 2013. Maximum tensile strength was 3.12 GPa; the corresponding resolved shear stress was 0.98 GPa, compared with a calculated ideal shear strength of 1.42 GPa. This establishes laboratory progress through a shear-strength comparison.
milestones.set_by: Ultra-strength convention summarized by Zhang and colleagues in Science Advances in 2016, following the earlier ultra-strength literature.

milestones.title: A metal specimen sustains tensile stress exceeding half its matched ideal tensile strength.
milestones.criterion: At laboratory specimen size, measured specimen-wide tensile stress exceeds 0.5 times the ideal tensile strength of the corresponding defect-free crystal. Composition, phase, direction, stress measure and calculation boundary conditions must make the ratio interpretable. The published deep ultra-strength definition supplies the fraction. The 2013 gold-nanowire paper bears on this stage, but its first-principles comparison concerns ideal shear strength; that comparison alone does not establish the required tensile ratio.
milestones.set_by: Deep ultra-strength definition introduced by Zhang and colleagues in Science Advances in 2016 for silicon nanowires; the original demonstration concerned silicon.
milestones.threshold_quote: exceeding one-half of the bulk ideal strength

milestones.title: A 12.5 mm diameter metal specimen sustains more than half its ideal tensile strength.
milestones.criterion: A metal specimen with initial diameter 12.5 ± 0.2 mm and gauge length 62.5 ± 0.1 mm sustains true axial tensile stress above 0.5 times its matched ideal tensile strength at a specified temperature within 10–38 °C. The dimensions are the published standard ASTM round geometry. This stage establishes the strength result at that section size before adding the completion test's fatigue-precracked stable-tearing result. No qualifying demonstration was verified in the opened sources.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback: USMS and JSPS publish no numerical bulk-section achievement criterion. The strength fraction comes from the deep ultra-strength definition and the dimensions from ASTM E8M-01e1; their combination is an Atlas choice.

not_found: No externally adopted combined strength-fraction, section-size and crack-resistance threshold was found in USMS, JSPS project 23K20037 or DARPA INTACT documents.
No minimum fracture toughness accompanies the published deep ultra-strength definition.
No qualifying combined demonstration was verified; this does not establish worldwide nonachievement.
Current ASTM publisher pages were accessible, but complete current editions were not; the opened older editions supplied the specimen geometry and stable-tearing definition.
The publisher page for the 2025 perspective could not be fetched; its complete PMC version was opened.

results.finding: Gold nanowires (more than 20 tested) reached 0.69 times the ideal shear strength.
results.detail: Nanowires were 8–20 nm in diameter. The maximum resolved shear stress was 0.98 GPa, compared with an ideal shear strength of 1.42 GPa; the highest-strength wires fractured in a brittle-like manner.
results.quote:
Remarkably, this limit corres-
ponds to a critical resolved shear stress of 0.98 GPa for partial
{111}o1124 slip (Schmid factor ¼ 0.314), which is very close to
the ideal shear strength of 1.42 GPa for pure Au reported from
past ﬁrst-principle calculations 27.

results.finding: Single-crystal Cu nanowhiskers, 75–300 nm in diameter, fractured at tensile stresses of 1–7 GPa.
results.detail: The measured tensile strengths bear on the milestone, but the comparison given is to theoretical shear strength. No matched ideal tensile strength or interpretable tensile-strength ratio is provided.
results.quote:
Apparent brittle fracture occurred at stresses lying between
1 and 7 GPa (Figure 3d).

results.finding: Ultratwinned gold nanowires, 8–20 nm in diameter, reached tensile strengths up to 3.12 GPa.
results.detail: The reported stress is engineering stress. The first-principles comparison is to ideal shear strength, not matched ideal tensile strength; the simulated 5.5 GPa tensile estimate is described as an upper limit.
results.quote:
exhibit tensile strengths up to 3.12 GPa, near the ideal limit, with a remarkable ductile-to-
brittle transition with decreasing twin size.

results.finding: Cu nanowhiskers, number of specimens not reported, fractured at tensile stresses of 1–7 GPa.
results.detail: Whiskers were 75–300 nm in diameter. Resolved shear stresses were reported as consistent with theoretical shear strengths, but no matched numerical ideal strength or ratio was given.
results.quote:
Apparent brittle fracture occurred at stresses lying between
1 and 7 GPa (Figure 3d).

results.finding: Molybdenum nanocrystals, 25–90 nm apex diameter: maximum tensile strength 19.8 GPa.
results.detail: The 〈110〉-oriented specimens were tested at 77 K and failed plastically. The tested region was nanoscale, and the text does not establish a matched ideal tensile-strength ratio for the measured maximum.
results.quote: The experimental values of tensile strength vary between 6.3 and 19.8 GPa and show a decrease with increasing nanorod diameter.

results.finding: Single-crystal nickel nanoparticles, approximately 210 nm in diameter, reached 34 GPa compressive strength; the number tested was not stated.
results.detail: The peak resolved shear stress was estimated at about 10 GPa, versus a 15.4 GPa theoretical shear-strength estimate. The reported compressive stress is load divided by initial contact area; the text does not establish that stress exceeded the threshold throughout the specimen.
results.quote:
The most remarkable ﬁnding is the ultrahigh compressive
strength of the Ni nanoparticles reaching 34 GPa ( D ≈ 210 nm).
